gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much AC energy each kit actually delivers when measured: the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 put about 1,990 Wh into a 987 W heater (96% of its 2,073.6 Wh rating, APH Networks). OutdoorGearLab measured 82–87% on the 1 kWh rivals (AC180 950 Wh, Jackery 1000 v2 910 Wh, Anker C1000 Gen 2 890 Wh), so the Elite gives about 2.1–2.2× their usable energy, compared with 1.8–2.0× on the rated figures.
standout_why: I compared against the four cited pages. backup-power.org already normalises cycle life (it flags Jackery's 70% end point against 80% for EcoFlow and BLUETTI, and notes that the Elite 200 V2's '6,000+' has no end point), so cycle life is not new. It also normalises lifting against continuous AC output for the Elite 200 V2 (2,600 W continuous, 3,900 W resistive only). None of its figures are measured. EnergySage says it tested nothing and has no capacity or cycle figures for any model. Our current Dealectric page gives only rated Wh and a 'fridge + CPAP' range with no measured basis. I could not fetch Good Housekeeping (the fetch tool is blocked there), so I can't rule out that it has a capacity test. None of the uncited top results were opened.
decides: This confirms the Elite 200 V2 as the pick on the measure that matters most in a multi-day outage: stored energy you can use before the sun returns. Rated Wh says it holds 1.80× an AC180. Measured AC output says 2.09× (1,990 Wh against 950 Wh). Station-only prices on BLUETTI's US store today work out to about 2.21 Wh per dollar for the Elite 200 V2 ($899) and 1.90 for the AC180 ($499). Footnote for the table: the Elite figure comes from a different lab and load (APH, 987 W heater) than the OutdoorGearLab light-bar figures, and the AC180 was run at 80% load. Treat the gap as approximate, not exact.

findings.label: Measured AC energy delivered, full to shutoff
findings.value: ≈1,990 Wh at the load (96.0% of 2,073.6 Wh); APH states 2,028 Wh (97.8%)
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 Review (Page 4 of 5) – APH Networks
findings.note: APH ran an electric heater drawing a constant 987 W through the AC outlet, and it ran 2 h 1 min. 987 W × 2.0167 h ≈ 1,990 Wh. APH's 2,028 Wh uses the unit's own display reading of 1,006 W (1,006 × 2.0167 ≈ 2,029). I use the heater-side figure because it is the conservative one. The review page gives no date.

findings.label: Measured usable AC capacity
findings.note: OutdoorGearLab used a light-bar test jig 'at 80% load until it fully drained', about 1,440 W of the 1,800 W rating. Review dated 2026-01-13. The page also says one 200 W panel gives a full charge in '6-8 hours under ideal conditions'.
